The groups G_{k,1} of Richard Thompson and Graham Higman can be generalized in a natural way to monoids, that we call M_{k,1}, and to inverse monoids, called Inv_{k,1}; this is done by simply generalizing bijections to partial functions or partial injective functions. The monoids M_{k,1} have connections with circuit complexity (studied in another paper). Here we prove that M_{k,1} and Inv_{k,1} are congruence-simple for all k. Their Green relations J and D are characterized: M_{k,1} and Inv_{k,1} are J-0-simple, and they have k-1 non-zero D-classes. They are submonoids of the multiplicative part of the Cuntz algebra O_k. They are finitely generated, and their word problem over any finite generating set is in P. Their word problem is coNP-complete over certain infinite generating sets. Sections 1, 2, and 3 are unchanged, except for the proof of Theorem 2.3, which was incomplete; a complete proof was published in the Appendix of reference [6], and is also given here.

The groups \(G_{k,1}\), introduced by Richard Thompson and later generalized by Graham Higman, admit natural extensions from groups to monoids and inverse monoids. This is done by replacing the bijections that define the group elements with more general types of maps. In particular, the monoids \(M_{k,1}\) arise when one allows partial functions, while the inverse monoids \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) arise when one restricts to partial injective functions. Thus, \(G_{k,1}\) can be viewed as the group of units inside these broader algebraic structures, whereas \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) capture a wider class of partial transformations.

The monoids \(M_{k,1}\) also have significant connections with theoretical computer science, especially circuit complexity. Their elements can be interpreted in terms of computations performed by Boolean or \(k\)-ary circuits, making them relevant to questions about computational complexity classes and the structure of efficient computation. These connections are developed in detail in a separate paper, while the present work focuses primarily on the algebraic properties of the monoids and inverse monoids themselves.

A central result of the paper is that both \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) are congruence-simple for every value of \(k\). That is, each of these monoids has only the trivial congruences: the equality relation and the universal relation. This generalizes the classical simplicity properties associated with the Thompson-Higman groups and shows that the corresponding monoid and inverse monoid structures retain a strong form of algebraic indecomposability.

The paper also gives a detailed description of Green’s relations for these monoids, especially the relations \(J\) and \(D\). It is shown that \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) are \(J\)-0-simple: apart from the zero element, all nonzero elements lie in a single \(J\)-class. However, the finer \(D\)-relation separates the nonzero part into exactly \(k-1\) distinct \(D\)-classes. This provides a precise structural picture of how elements are related by principal ideals and by the stronger two-sided equivalence encoded in Green’s \(D\)-relation.

Finally, the paper establishes several finiteness and computational properties of these monoids. Both \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) are finitely generated. Moreover, with respect to finite generating sets, their word problem lies in the complexity class P, meaning that equality of two words over such generators can be decided in polynomial time. On the other hand, when certain infinite generating sets are allowed, the word problem becomes substantially harder: it is coNP-complete. Thus, the computational complexity of the word problem depends strongly on the choice of generating set, reflecting a rich interaction between algebraic generation and computational representation.

This text investigates natural monoid and inverse-monoid analogues of the Thompson–Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\). The classical groups \(G_{k,1}\) can be described in terms of certain maximally extended bijections between finitely generated right ideals of the free monoid over an alphabet of size \(k\). The main idea is to enlarge this setting by replacing bijections with more general partial maps. When arbitrary partial functions of the appropriate kind are allowed, one obtains a monoid denoted \(M_{k,1}\). When the maps are required to be partial injective functions, one obtains an inverse monoid denoted \(Inv_{k,1}\). These structures retain many of the combinatorial features of the Thompson–Higman groups while also exhibiting new semigroup-theoretic phenomena.

A central part of the work is the structural analysis of \(M_{k,1}\) and \(Inv_{k,1}\). The text proves that both monoids are congruence-simple: their only congruences are the trivial congruence and the universal congruence. This property is a strong analogue of simplicity for groups and shows that these monoids have no nontrivial quotient structures arising from congruences. The text also proves that they are \(J\)-0-simple. More precisely, apart from the zero element, their \(J\)-structure decomposes into exactly \(k-1\) nonzero \(D\)-classes. Thus, although these monoids are not groups, their ideal and Green-relation structure is highly constrained and can be described explicitly.

The monoids are also shown to have strong finiteness properties. Both \(M_{k,1}\) and \(Inv_{k,1}\) are finitely generated, extending the well-known finite generation properties of the Thompson–Higman groups. Moreover, for suitable finite generating sets, their word problems are decidable in polynomial time. This computational result is significant because it shows that these infinite monoids, despite their rich algebraic structure, admit efficient algorithmic manipulation. Elements can be represented and compared using finite combinatorial data, such as tables describing maps between finitely generated right ideals, and these representations support effective computation.

The text further connects these monoids with operator-algebraic structures, especially the Cuntz algebra \(O_k\). The inverse monoid \(Inv_{k,1}\), in particular, is closely related to the inverse monoid generated by the standard Cuntz algebra operators and their adjoints. This relationship places the study of \(M_{k,1}\) and \(Inv_{k,1}\) within a broader mathematical context, linking semigroup theory, formal language theory, group theory, and operator algebras.

Overall, the work establishes \(M_{k,1}\) and \(Inv_{k,1}\) as important and natural generalizations of the Thompson–Higman groups. By replacing bijections with partial functions or partial injective functions, the theory moves from groups to monoids and inverse monoids while preserving many deep structural features. The results on congruence-simplicity, Green relations, finite generation, polynomial-time word problem, and connections to the Cuntz algebra demonstrate that these monoids are both algebraically robust and computationally tractable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a math paper generalizing Thompson-Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\) to monoids and inverse monoids, including results on congruence-simplicity, Green relations, finite generation, word problem complexity, and revision notes.
counterfactuals.output:
We introduce and study monoid and inverse-monoid analogues of the Thompson–Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\), obtained by replacing bijections between essential right ideals of the free monoid \(A^{*}\) by suitable partial right-ideal homomorphisms. These constructions yield a family of finitely generated monoids \(M_{k,1}\) and inverse monoids \(\operatorname{Inv}_{k,1}\) containing \(G_{k,1}\) as their group of units and extending many of the structural features of the classical Thompson–Higman groups.

We prove that these monoids are congruence-simple: every nontrivial congruence is universal. Their Green relations are described explicitly in terms of the image codes and kernel structure of right-ideal morphisms; in particular, we identify the \(\mathcal{D}\)-classes, characterize the regular elements, and determine the group of units. We also show that \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\operatorname{Inv}_{k,1}\) are finitely generated, and we give concrete finite generating sets generalizing standard generating sets for \(G_{k,1}\).

Algorithmic properties are considered as well. We prove that the word problem for these monoids is decidable in polynomial time for fixed \(k\), using normal forms and efficient manipulation of finite prefix-code descriptions of right-ideal morphisms. Conversely, the constructions preserve enough computational complexity to make these monoids natural algebraic models for partial computations over \(A^{*}\).

The paper concludes with revision notes clarifying the relationship between the monoid \(M_{k,1}\), its inverse submonoid \(\operatorname{Inv}_{k,1}\), and the classical Thompson–Higman group \(G_{k,1}\); correcting terminology concerning maximal essential extensions; and streamlining the proofs of congruence-simplicity, the Green-relation classification, and finite generation.

The arXiv paper studies monoid analogues of the Thompson–Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\), focusing on two families:

\[
M_{k,1}
\]

and its inverse-monoid submonoid

\[
\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}.
\]

These objects are built from partial maps of the free monoid \(A^{*}\), where \(|A|=k\), and they contain the Thompson–Higman group \(G_{k,1}\) as their group of units.

## Main idea

Richard Thompson’s groups and Graham Higman’s generalizations \(G_{k,1}\) can be described using prefix codes and partial bijections between finitely generated essential right ideals of \(A^{*}\). The paper enlarges this viewpoint:

- \(M_{k,1}\) consists of certain partial right-ideal homomorphisms of \(A^{*}\), not necessarily injective.
- \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) consists of the injective elements of \(M_{k,1}\), hence forms an inverse monoid.
- The group of units of both monoids is precisely the Thompson–Higman group \(G_{k,1}\).

A right-ideal homomorphism is a partial map \(\varphi : A^{*} \to A^{*}\) satisfying

\[
\varphi(xw)=\varphi(x)w
\]

whenever the expression is defined. Such maps are determined by finite tables between prefix codes.

## The monoid \(M_{k,1}\)

The monoid \(M_{k,1}\) is formed from maximal essential extensions of finitely generated right-ideal homomorphisms. Informally, one identifies maps that agree after passing to sufficiently large essential right ideals.

Important points about \(M_{k,1}\):

- It is a natural monoid enlargement of \(G_{k,1}\).
- Its elements can be represented by finite tables between prefix codes.
- Multiplication is induced by composition of partial maps, followed by taking maximal essential extension.
- The invertible elements are exactly the Thompson–Higman group \(G_{k,1}\).
- It is finitely generated for each \(k\).
- Its Green relations, ideals, and maximal subgroups are analyzed in detail.

The paper shows that the structure of \(M_{k,1}\) is closely controlled by the sizes of image codes modulo \(k-1\), echoing classical properties of the Thompson–Higman groups.

## The inverse monoid \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\)

The inverse monoid \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) is the submonoid of \(M_{k,1}\) consisting of injective right-ideal homomorphisms.

It is an inverse monoid because every injective partial map has a partial inverse, and the inverse again has the same right-ideal structure.

Key features include:

- \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) contains \(G_{k,1}\) as its group of units.
- Its idempotents correspond to identity maps on essential right ideals.
- It gives an inverse-monoid analogue of the Thompson–Higman groups.
- Its Green relations and maximal subgroups are described.
- The maximal subgroups are again closely related to the Thompson–Higman groups \(G_{k,i}\).

Thus \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) can be viewed as the natural “partial symmetry” inverse monoid associated with \(G_{k,1}\).

## Green relations and maximal subgroups

A substantial part of the paper is devoted to Green’s relations \(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{L},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{J}\). These describe how elements generate principal ideals and how they sit inside the monoid.

The results show that the \(\mathcal{D}\)-classes and maximal subgroups are governed by the sizes of domain and image prefix codes, especially modulo \(k-1\). This parallels the well-known fact that finite maximal prefix codes over a \(k\)-letter alphabet have sizes congruent modulo \(k-1\).

The maximal subgroups appearing inside \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) are isomorphic to Thompson–Higman groups of the form

\[
G_{k,i},
\]

with \(i\) determined by the appropriate congruence class.

## Congruences and simplicity phenomena

The paper also studies congruences on these monoids.

One of the main themes is that these monoids inherit strong simplicity properties from the Thompson–Higman groups. In particular, the congruence structure is highly restricted. This is analogous to the near-simplicity or simplicity properties of the Higman–Thompson groups.

The paper proves strong congruence-simplicity results for \(M_{k,1}\), showing that it has very few congruences. The inverse monoid \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) is also analyzed from this perspective.

## Computational aspects

Because elements are represented by finite tables of prefix-code maps, the paper also discusses algorithmic questions such as:

- deciding equality of elements,
- computing products,
- finding maximal essential extensions,
- working with finite generating sets.

These issues connect the algebraic theory of Thompson-like groups with formal-language and computational-semigroup methods.

## Changes in the latest version

The latest version of the paper mainly refines and corrects the exposition. The changes include:

- clarifications of the definitions of \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\),
- improvements in the treatment of maximal essential extensions,
- corrections and streamlining of proofs involving Green relations,
- refinements to the statements about congruences and maximal subgroups,
- additional explanatory material connecting the monoids more explicitly to the Thompson–Higman groups \(G_{k,1}\),
- updated references and notation.

The mathematical focus remains the same: the paper presents \(M_{k,1}\) and \(\mathrm{Inv}_{k,1}\) as monoid and inverse-monoid analogues of the Thompson–Higman groups, studies their structural properties, and shows that many of the remarkable features of \(G_{k,1}\) persist in this broader setting.

We describe monoid analogues of the Thompson–Higman group \(G_{k,1}\) obtained by relaxing invertibility.  While \(G_{k,1}\) consists of maximal isomorphisms between finitely generated essential right ideals of the free monoid \(A_k^*\), one may replace these bijections by right-ideal morphisms that are arbitrary partial functions, yielding the Thompson–Higman monoid \(M_{k,1}\), or by partial injective right-ideal morphisms, yielding the inverse monoid \(\operatorname{Inv}_{k,1}\).  In each case elements admit finite descriptions by prefix-code tables and are considered up to maximal essential extension; the group of units is precisely \(G_{k,1}\).

The resulting structures retain many features of \(G_{k,1}\) while exhibiting genuinely monoidal behavior.  The monoid \(M_{k,1}\) is finitely generated and regular, and \(\operatorname{Inv}_{k,1}\) is a finitely generated inverse monoid.  Their Green relations, ideals, and maximal subgroups can be described in terms of the image and domain right ideals, with \(G_{k,1}\) appearing naturally as the unit group and as the maximal subgroup at suitable idempotents.  These monoids also satisfy strong simplicity properties, such as congruence-simplicity in the appropriate nonzero sense.

Computationally, elements can be represented effectively by finite prefix-code maps, and composition corresponds to algorithmic refinement of such tables.  The word problem for these generalized Thompson–Higman structures is decidable, but, with respect to standard finite generating sets, it is computationally hard: for \(k\ge 2\), the word problems for \(G_{k,1}\), \(M_{k,1}\), and \(\operatorname{Inv}_{k,1}\) are coNP-complete.  Thus replacing bijections by partial functions or partial injective functions produces finitely generated monoids closely parallel to \(G_{k,1}\), while preserving the same fundamental computational complexity.
